summary.text: An alkane is an acyclic saturated hydrocarbon: hydrogen and carbon atoms in a tree structure where every carbon–carbon bond is single.
Alkanes follow the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, running from methane (CH₄) to large and complex molecules.
Their two main commercial sources are petroleum and natural gas, and most alkanes do not have much biological activity.

facts.label: Wax size
facts.value: Over about 17 carbons in the backbone

facts.label: Mass step
facts.value: Members differ by multiples of 14.03 u

items.prompt: Cyclobutane is a four-carbon ring (C₄H₈) and butane is a four-carbon chain (C₄H₁₀). Are they isomers of each other?

options.label: Yes, because both are built from exactly four carbons
No, because they have different numbers of hydrogen atoms
Yes, because a ring is only a chain bent into a new shape
No, because only chains can be built from carbon atoms

items.explain: Forming a ring changes the number of rings and so the molecular formula, which is why cyclobutane is not an isomer of butane.

items.prompt: Two alkane isomers are compared: one is a straight chain and one is highly branched. Which is expected to be the more thermodynamically stable?

options.label: The straight chain, since it has the simplest shape
Neither; isomers always have identical stability
The highly branched one
The straight chain, since branches add strain to every alkane

items.explain: Branched alkanes are more thermodynamically stable than their linear isomers, as shown by 2,2,3,3-tetramethylbutane versus n-octane.

items.prompt: A sample is a ring of carbon atoms joined only by single bonds. Under the IUPAC definition, is it an alkane?

options.label: Yes, because every saturated hydrocarbon counts as an alkane
Yes, because its carbon–carbon bonds are all single bonds
No, because rings of carbon cannot be saturated with hydrogen
No, because IUPAC reserves the word for acyclic hydrocarbons

items.explain: IUPAC defines alkanes as acyclic, though some sources use the word for any saturated hydrocarbon, including cycloalkanes.

items.prompt: A biochemist says an alkane chain mostly serves as a frame inside living molecules. What does the frame carry?

options.label: More active and reactive functional groups of biological molecules
The alkane's own strong biological activity, which drives the molecule
Only the methane gas that archaea give off as a waste product
A set of identical alkane units that make the molecule reactive

items.explain: Most alkanes have little biological activity, so they work like molecular trees on which reactive functional groups hang.

items.prompt: A chemist wants a waxy alkane that stays solid at ordinary room temperature and pressure. Which one is the best pick?

options.label: One with a backbone of 5 carbon atoms
One with a backbone of 2 carbon atoms
One with a backbone of 30 carbon atoms
One with a backbone of 12 carbon atoms

items.explain: Alkane waxes are solids at standard ambient temperature and pressure and have a backbone of more than about 17 carbons.

items.prompt: A diagram shows a piece taken from an alkane, with one open spot where it can bond to something else. What is this fragment called?

options.label: An alkenyl group
An alkyl group
An aryl group
A cycloalkane

items.explain: An alkyl group is an alkane-based fragment bearing one open valence for bonding, unlike alkenyl or aryl groups.

paragraphs.heading: What an alkane is
paragraphs.text: An alkane is a saturated hydrocarbon with no rings. Its hydrogen and carbon atoms are arranged like a branching tree, and every bond between two carbons is a single bond. Alkanes follow the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, so they run from methane, CH₄, where n is 1, up to very large molecules such as hexacontane, C₆₀H₁₂₂. An older, historical name for them is paraffin.

paragraphs.heading: Inside the molecule
paragraphs.text: Every carbon in an alkane is sp³-hybridized and forms four sigma bonds, each to either another carbon or a hydrogen. Each hydrogen is bonded to one carbon. The longest chain of linked carbons is called the carbon skeleton or carbon backbone, and the number of carbons can be taken as the size of the alkane. A typical carbon–carbon single bond is 1.53 ångströms long.

paragraphs.heading: A ladder of sizes
paragraphs.text: With their repeating –CH₂ units, alkanes form a homologous series, a family whose members differ in mass by multiples of 14.03 u. Each step is the mass of one carbon atom, 12.01 u, plus two hydrogen atoms of about 1.01 u each. Among the higher alkanes are the waxes, which have more than about 17 carbons in the backbone and are solid at standard room temperature and pressure.

paragraphs.heading: Branches and isomers
paragraphs.text: Saturated hydrocarbons can be linear, branched or ring-shaped. Branched alkanes are more thermodynamically stable than their straighter isomers: n-octane, a straight chain, is about 1.9 kcal/mol less stable than its highly branched isomer 2,2,3,3-tetramethylbutane. Some branched alkanes are chiral, such as 3-methylhexane, which has a stereogenic center at carbon number 3. Closing a ring changes the formula, so cyclobutane, C₄H₈, is not an isomer of butane, C₄H₁₀.

paragraphs.heading: Naming straight chains
paragraphs.text: Unbranched alkanes are named with a Greek number prefix for how many carbons they have, plus the ending -ane. The first four names came instead from methanol, ether, propionic acid and butyric acid. From five carbons on, the ending is added to the number prefix: pentane is C₅H₁₂, hexane C₆H₁₄, heptane C₇H₁₆ and octane C₈H₁₈. Counts ending in nine break the pattern with a Latin prefix, as in nonane.

paragraphs.heading: Naming branched chains
paragraphs.text: Straight chains sometimes get the prefix n-, for normal, to set them apart from branched forms, as in n-butane versus isobutane. Simple branched alkanes often have common names, so the three forms of pentane are n-pentane, isopentane and neopentane. For a systematic name, number the longest continuous chain so the side chains get the lowest numbers, and name each side chain by turning -ane into -yl.

paragraphs.heading: Quiet frameworks
paragraphs.text: Most alkanes have little biological activity. Still, methanogenic archaea make methane, and some long-chain alkanes act as pheromones in certain animals or as protective waxes in plants and fungi. Alkanes can be pictured as frameworks on which the more reactive functional groups of biological molecules hang. Commercially, they come mainly from petroleum and natural gas.
